Summary: The paper builds a benchmark for writing OMIM phenotype entries from exactly the papers the curators cited (100 entries, 515 papers, 19% readable in full text via open access), holding the model (Claude Opus 5.5), guards, a claim-level citation audit and the scoring fixed while varying only the generation strategy: direct reading of all papers in one prompt, an agentic curator with read/search tools, an evidence graph, a per-patient case table, recall-then-verify, a memory-only control, and three add-ons (second-hand passages, a reconciled case database, a learned curation guide). The primary endpoint is coverage of 6,652 facts split once, without sight of any draft, from OMIM's allelic-variant paragraphs deposited in ClinVar. Main results: hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (46 entries; Fig. 2a, Table 22); reading strategies convey 91.0-94.4% of facts the supplied text is judged to state and 5.5-6.9% of those it does not (Fig. 2c); the agent and evidence graph are not distinguishable from direct reading, the case table trails by 1.9 points (Table 1); a per-paper completeness pass adds 2.6 points on 38 held-out entries (Sec. 4.3, Fig. 3b); released PaperQA2 and GraphRAG pipelines convey fewer facts on 10 and 4 entries (Sec. 4.4); and the audit catches planted citation swaps and single-value substitutions but not added citations, omissions or most deleted qualifiers (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 4). Every fact split, coverage judgement, 'stated' judgement and audit verdict is made by the writer's own model family, and no human validated any of them.
Strengths: Clean controlled design: the same papers, model, guards, audit and scoring are used for every strategy, so the generation strategy is the only variable (Sec. 3, Fig. 1). Few comparisons of RAG, graph, agentic and long-context designs hold this much fixed, and none I know of does it for knowledge-base writing against curator text.

The within-paper access manipulation (hiding the full text of the same 91 papers and rewriting from abstracts, with and without second-hand passages; Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2a, Table 22) is a real causal design that separates access from paper identity, and it reports the like-for-like comparison with no arm repaired.

Measurement hygiene is careful and useful to others: fact lists are fixed once before any draft is seen, and the paper shows that splitting afresh per draft inflates levels by 2-5 points (Table 5); completion is treated symmetrically, with an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis (Table 10); judge variation and run-to-run replicate noise are measured separately from the between-entry bootstrap (App. E, Table 19); and an earlier asymmetric analysis that put the evidence graph 2.1 points behind is reported as corrected (App. M.4).

Statistical reporting is restrained: paired bootstrap intervals, exact sign tests, Holm adjustment for secondary measures, entries better/worse/tied, and an explicit statement that the non-significant differences are not an equivalence claim because no margin was set in advance (Sec. 4.2).

The audit stress test turns up a concrete, actionable design flaw: taking a claim's best verdict over its cited papers makes added irrelevant citations invisible (0/30 flagged although the added paper's own verdict was 'unsupported' for all 176 claims; Sec. 4.5, Fig. 4, Table 47). It also shows that omissions are invisible to fidelity audits by construction. Both points matter beyond this domain for citation-verification pipelines.

The reading-better arms were designed on three training entries and frozen before the 41 held-out entries were run, with Holm adjustment across arms and a fidelity check on 20 audited entries (Sec. 4.3, Table 30). This is the cleanest positive result in the paper.

Negative results, losses to safety-filter stops and corrected analyses are reported openly, with a full ledger of every experiment and why entries dropped out (Table 2). The harness, drafts, verdicts and scores are released, and the reference can be rebuilt from public resources.
Weaknesses: No judgement is validated by a person, and one model family does everything: it writes, extracts, splits the reference into facts, judges each fact present/partly/absent, judges whether the supplied text states each fact, and audits the claims (Sec. 3.3; Limitations (i)). The 95.7% agreement between two judgings (App. E) measures self-consistency, not validity. Self-preference (Panickssery et al., 2024) and blind spots shared by writer and judge could shift absolute levels, the stated/not-stated split, and the audit's apparent sensitivity. An expert annotation of a few hundred facts and audit verdicts, with chance-corrected agreement, would be the single most valuable addition and is missing.

The headline 'access bounds agreement' is mostly expected (the paper says so in Sec. 1), and part of its evidence is close to circular. The 91-94% vs <7% contrast (Fig. 2c) conditions on a model judgement that the text 'states' a fact, which requires a verified quote. Facts the model can quote from the text are the ones a reader of that text conveys, and facts that need inference or paraphrase are more likely to be classed as not stated. The hidden-full-text experiment (79.8% vs 36.1%) is the clean evidence, but it measures the size of an obvious effect rather than giving new insight.

The tested regime favours direct reading: 2-12 references, median input about 39k characters, all papers fitting in one prompt (Sec. 3.1, Sec. 4.4). The regime where intermediate representations or agents might plausibly separate (many relevant papers) has no usable comparison: App. M.1 draws no findings from 10 entries, and K.2 compares zero entries because of safety-filter stops. So the near-null differences between designs do not generalise beyond small reference sets, and the discussion's argument that the measurement could have resolved them is, by the authors' own description, 'an observation, not a test' (Sec. 5).

Conclusions about paradigms rest on one in-house implementation each, developed on the evaluation entries themselves (Limitations (vi)). The case table's deficit shrinks from -2.3 to -0.2 points when extraction effort is raised and the writer chooses synopsis terms (Sec. 4.2, App. F), and in the same ablation the evidence graph moves above direct reading (+1.8). The ranking therefore depends on settings and implementation choices, not only on the representation, which weakens statements such as 'no other design conveyed more than direct reading'.

The reference is narrow and indirect: variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs deposited in ClinVar, not the phenotype entries' narrative sections. Only about 24% of a draft's statements have a counterpart in it (App. H; Limitations (ii)). The primary endpoint is recall on a thin slice of what an entry says, and the relevance and precision of the remaining ~76% of each draft rest only on the self-audit. The framing 'knowledge-base writing' in the title and abstract claims more than this endpoint measures.

Missingness from safety-filter stops is non-random and cannot be inspected: 7 of 100 main entries, 10 of 30 entries from 2026, all 4 large entries, and every STORM entry (Table 2). Stops may correlate with disease topic or content. Restricting comparisons to entries every strategy completed can bias them, and the case-table result already moves from -1.9 (-3.1, -0.8) to -1.4 (-4.2, +1.4) under the intention-to-treat rule (Sec. 4.2, Table 10). The paper does not characterise which entries or papers are stopped.

Only one proprietary model is evaluated, with no temperature or seed control (Sec. 3.2, App. B). With no second model family, as writer or as judge, it is unknown whether the strategy ordering or the access effect transfers, in particular to smaller-context or weaker models, where extraction-first designs are usually motivated. For a paper whose main contribution is a benchmark, a single-model evaluation limits how useful the benchmark is shown to be.

The released-pipeline comparison is not like for like and is too small to support statements in the introduction (Sec. 1, Sec. 4.4, App. J). PaperQA2 and GraphRAG are question-answering systems that answered six section questions whose answers were concatenated; PaperQA2 ran without its agent because the adapter lacks function calling; only the authors' drafts went through repair; and n = 10, 4 and 0 entries. The paper's own caveats ('no ranking of the systems') are appropriate, but the result should not appear among the headline claims.

Contamination remains a live confound for the reading results. Memory alone conveys 24.1% of facts in the 600000-609999 band, and direct reading's coverage of abstract-only papers falls from 49.8% to 37.9% with creation era (Sec. 4.2, Tables 14-15). The 2026 check rests on 20 compared entries, and the training cut-off is unknown (App. M.2). Absolute coverage levels, and some of the 'conveyed from abstract-only papers' provenance (Table 17: 1.7% in no supplied text, 10.0% for partial facts), therefore mix reading with recall.

Multiplicity and post hoc restrictions: the primary endpoint is not adjusted across the five comparisons, and the paper calls the case-table deficit on facts stated in full-text papers (-8.4 on 40 entries; Sec. 4.2) 'the stronger evidence'. That is a restriction analysis not stated to be pre-specified. Many subgroup, era and access-group analyses are reported alongside, so the main claims should be tied explicitly to pre-specified tests.

The audit stress test is small and partly easy. The qualifier-deletion rules have 2-8 items each, swaps are mostly between papers on different topics, all planted errors sit in evidence-graph paragraphs, and the controls are paragraphs that had already passed (Fig. 4, Table 47). The best-verdict flaw is diagnosed but not fixed, and no per-paper aggregation rule is evaluated for its false-flag cost.

Presentation is very dense. Nearly every sentence carries several estimates, intervals, entry counts and caveats; the main text reads like a compressed results log; the appendix has 52 tables over about 40 pages; and key notions (pooled vs. mean over entries, 'stated', completion, repaired vs. unrepaired arms) are defined in scattered places. The main takeaways are hard to extract on a first read. Some noticeable patterns go undiscussed, for example direct reading's much lower coverage in the classic 1xxxxx-5xxxxx band (34.9% vs. 51-54% elsewhere; Table 15).

Fit and novelty for ICLR are modest. The compared methods are standard (long-context reading, GraphRAG-style graphs, agents, self-verification, prompt optimisation), and the generalisable lessons (full text beats abstracts; long context is competitive with intermediate representations when everything fits; best-verdict citation audits miss over-citation) mostly confirm known or expected results. The contribution is mainly a careful domain benchmark, which might fit better in a datasets-and-benchmarks or biomedical-informatics venue.
Questions: Can you provide a human (clinical geneticist or curator) validation on a random sample of facts: present/partly/absent judgements, 'stated' judgements and audit verdicts, with chance-corrected agreement? Do the main paired differences and the 91-94% vs <7% contrast survive with human labels?

Can you re-judge a subset with a different model family (ideally an open-weight model) and, separately, generate drafts with a second writer model, to test whether the strategy ordering and the access effect depend on the model?

How often does the 'stated' judgement mark as 'not stated' a fact that is inferable from the text but not quotable verbatim? A manual check of 50-100 'not stated' facts from full-text papers would show how much of the Fig. 2c contrast is mechanical.

How many prompt iterations were the main strategies developed through on the evaluation entries, and was any strategy's prompt tuned more than another's? Could you rerun the main comparison on a fresh held-out sample of the 2xxxxx-6xxxxx bands?

Which entries and papers trigger the safety-filter stops? Are they concentrated in particular disease areas (e.g., reproductive, oncologic or pediatric topics) or particular strategies' prompts, and how does that affect the completion-restricted comparison?

Is there a feasible way to test the many-relevant-papers regime, e.g., a model or deployment with fewer stops, or reference sets built from relevant OA papers, so that the claim that designs do not separate is tested where they are expected to?

How much does the entry header (title and alternative titles) reveal the withheld causal gene? The memory-only control already reaches 83.9% gene F1 (Table 1), which suggests the gene measure is near ceiling for reasons other than reading.
Why is direct reading's coverage so much lower in the classic band (34.9%; Table 15)? Is this access, older OCR'd text, or a property of older OMIM variant paragraphs?

Have you evaluated a per-paper verdict aggregation rule for the audit (flag a claim when any cited paper is judged unsupported)? What is its false-flag rate on the real multi-citation paragraphs, where 4-7% of (claim, paper) pairs are already judged not to support the claim?

For the case-table result, was the restriction to facts stated in full-text papers specified before the results were seen? If not, could the -1.9 point result be reported as the confirmatory test and the restrictions as exploratory?
Limitations: The authors list the main limitations candidly (Sec. 5): one model family for everything, no human validation, a narrow reference, open-access text only, the reference list given, strategies developed on the evaluation entries, stops, few references per entry, a small audit stress test, released systems at one setting, and list-price costs.

Not sufficiently addressed: the possible circularity of conditioning coverage on a same-model 'stated' judgement that requires a verbatim quote, which may mechanically inflate the stated/not-stated contrast.

Not sufficiently addressed: results are specific to one implementation per paradigm and to the chosen effort settings (App. F shows that settings move the case table by about 2 points), so paradigm-level conclusions should be scoped accordingly.
Not sufficiently addressed: the selection bias from non-random, unobservable safety-filter stops, including whether stopped content is topic-related.

Not sufficiently addressed: leakage of the withheld causal gene through entry headers and memorisation of OMIM content, which affect absolute levels on the secondary measures and the provenance analysis.

Societal: the drafts concern clinical genetics; the paper rightly says they are not clinical guidance and must not be presented as OMIM content. Downstream users should be warned that a fidelity audit passes a draft that faithfully copies a source's error and does not detect omissions.
